meta.title: Buddhist Bridges — India–Korea Buddhist Connections: Interactive Timeline (MVP)
meta.basis: Frozen V3.0 + validated derived tables (analysis/data) + prosopography outputs. Explicit dates only; APPROX ranges are visually fuzzy; undated records are unplaced, never dated.

card.profession_role: Buddhist monk; pilgrim; translator
card.religious_affiliation: Buddhism (Esoteric/Vajrayana; disciple of Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra)
card.institution_org: Juefu Temple (Chang'an); Dryuan Puti Temple (Mt Wutai)
card.travel_summary: Departed Guangzhou by sea (c. 719 or 723); toured the Five Indias; reached Nishapur (Persia); returned overland via Pamir/Central Asia; account ends at Kucha, Nov 727
card.evidence_of_influence: Wang ocheonchukguk jeon (往五天竺國傳), the sole surviving 8th-c. East Asian record of India/Central Asia; Dunhuang ms. (Pelliot 1908), Bibliothèque nationale de France
card.historical_significance: First Korean recorded to have travelled to India by sea and returned overland leaving a written record; 'world's oldest of the four great travelogues' per Korean scholarship
card.notes: Travel dates conflict across sources (719-727 vs 723-727/728; '730경' per our-history-net). Standard Korean dates 704-787 (Korean Wikipedia, NIKH-adjacent sources, 인천in); birth c. 700 / death 780 appear in older scholarship - kept as variant. Author identification with Amoghavajra's Silla disciple is scholarly consensus (Takakusu).
card.rationale: Core record: Silla pilgrim-monk; Wang ocheonchukguk jeon is the primary 8th-c. source on India

card.profession_role: Buddhist monk; Yogacara scholar; abbot
card.travel_summary: NULL (Silla->Tang c. 627 only; lived in Chang'an)
card.evidence_of_influence: Commentaries (e.g., on Samdhinirmocana-sutra) studied and quoted in Tibetan doxographies; long-standing rivalry with Kuiji
card.historical_significance: One of the most influential Silla monks in Tang China; his works transmitted to Tibet
card.notes: Dates 613-696 per John Powers (JIABS); some accounts differ slightly.
card.rationale: Silla Yogacara master; India link via Indian doctrine studied in Chang'an (no travel)

card.profession_role: Buddhist philosopher-monk; author; popularizer; founder of Haedongjong
card.travel_summary: Legend (hagiography): while travelling to Tang with Ŭisang, awakened overnight in a cave ('mind only') and never went abroad; no India journey recorded
card.evidence_of_influence: Haedong-so commentaries studied in Tang/Japan; called 'Jinna bosal' in China (equated with Indian logician Dignaga); T'ong pulgyo synthesis
card.historical_significance: Korea's greatest Buddhist philosopher; synthesized Indian/Chinese Buddhist thought for Korea
card.notes: Person and works verified; the cave legend is traditional hagiography. Relationship to India is intellectual, not physical.
card.rationale: Silla philosopher; commentaries on Indian-origin texts (Awakening of Faith)

card.profession_role: Buddhist monk ('foreign monk' 胡僧)
card.nationality_region: UNCERTAIN (Western Regions/Serindia; some scholars argue Indian; came via Eastern Jin China)
card.travel_summary: Came from Eastern Jin territory to Baekje by sea, 384 CE; no detailed itinerary preserved
card.evidence_of_influence: Samguk Sagi (sg_024r_0100_0030) and Samguk Yusa records; both mark 384 as the start of Baekje Buddhism
card.historical_significance: Traditional founder of Baekje Buddhism; earliest documented Buddhist arrival in Korean history
card.notes: Origin debated: db.history.go.kr (Samguk Sagi) notes '흔히 서역 출신으로 추정' with a minority view identifying him as an Indian monk (이상호 1960); encykorea describes him as '인도의 승려' (Gandhara-born per en-wiki); arrived via Eastern Jin. Sanskrit reconstruction of the name not attested in sources.
card.rationale: Earliest documented Buddhist arrival in Korea (384 CE); founder of Baekje Buddhism

card.profession_role: Indian Buddhist master; Seon/Chan patriarch
card.travel_summary: Magadha -> (Tibet) -> Yuan China -> Goryeo (1326) -> Yuan China; died 1363 (relics sent to Goryeo)

card.rationale: Flagship record: last great Indian monk in Korea; Nalanda -> Goryeo; founded Hoeamsa 1328; Naong's teacher

card.profession_role: Enlightenment thinker; historian; publisher; magazine editor
card.religious_affiliation: None (wrote on Buddhism as national culture)
card.travel_summary: Studied in Japan (Tokyo); met Tagore there 1916; never visited India
card.evidence_of_influence: budreview.com profile (Kim Young-jin 2013) quoting the India/Xiyu direct-route claim; beopbo.com on Chosŏn Pulgyo (2004); EncyKorea '통불교사상'
card.historical_significance: Cast Korea as the culmination (not periphery) of India-originated Buddhism in world civilizational history
card.notes: Beware the widespread 'Yuktang requested Song of the Defeated' myth - corrected by Hong Eun-taek (the request was made by Chin Hak-mun).
card.rationale: Wrote Choson Pulgyo (1930) arguing Buddhism reached Korea directly from India; nationalist framing; Tagore meeting 1916

card.profession_role: Poet; novelist; playwright; essayist; educator; first Asian Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)
card.travel_summary: Visited Japan five times (1916-1929) and China once (1924); never set foot in Korea despite two planned contacts; met Korean students in person in Tokyo/Yokohama 1916
card.evidence_of_influence: Dong-a Ilbo archival record; Hong Eun-taek's studies (2012, 2014); Choi Seong-woo's rhetorical analysis (2022); Kim Ujo (2014) in 인도연구; 2011 bust at Daehak-ro (gift of the Indian government)
card.historical_significance: The single most important Indian figure in Korean cultural memory of this period; his 'lamp' message became a national symbol of hope
card.notes: The famous 15-line 'poem' is a patchwork: Tagore's actual message was a 6-line English note (an apology for declining the lecture request), translated into 4 Korean lines by Chu Yo-han (Apr 1929); Gitanjali #35 was appended and 'Korea' inserted in a closing line Tagore never wrote (likely from 세계명시선 1977); circulated in 2002/2003 textbooks and inscribed under the 2011 bust. First poem actually sent to Koreans: 'The Song of the Defeated' (Fruit-Gathering no. 85, Jan 1916).
card.rationale: Channel figure: Lamp of the East (1929) invoked Korea's Buddhist heritage; influenced Han Yong-un; Seoul visit planned 1929, never made

card.profession_role: Buddhist monk-poet; independence activist
card.travel_summary: No India travel
card.evidence_of_influence: KCI comparative Han/Tagore study (ART002442623); Kim Ujo, 'Tagore's Perception of Joseon and Its Reception in Joseon', 인도연구 19(1), 2014
card.historical_significance: Emblematic case of Korean creative absorption of Tagore's spiritual lyricism transformed into national resistance poetry
card.notes: Dates widely documented; not re-pulled in pilot.
card.rationale: Buddhist monk-poet (PRIMARY identity); India link via Tagore's spiritual lyricism (literary-religious reception with critical distance)

card.profession_role: Lawyer; political and spiritual leader of the Indian independence movement

card.description: The BnF's Dunhuang manuscript of Hyecho's Wang ocheonchukguk jeon (往五天竺國傳) - the sole surviving 8th-century record of India by a Silla monk - was loaned to the National Museum of Korea for the '실크로드와 둔황: 혜초와 함께 하는 서역기행' special exhibition (18 Dec 2010 - 3 Apr 2011; manuscript on display until 17 Mar 2011 per the BnF's 3-month loan limit): the manuscript's first public display anywhere since Pelliot's 1908 Dunhuang discovery; a second BnF loan followed for the NMK exhibition Dec 2019 - Apr 2020
card.significance: World-first public display of Korea's oldest travel record of India; made Hyecho's 8th-century India pilgrimage tangible for the Korean public and scholars
card.evidence: National Museum of Korea archive (2010-06-29); KBS News 2010-12-17; Hani 2019-10-19 (second loan)
card.rationale: World-first public display of the BnF Wang ocheonchukguk jeon manuscript at NMK (2010-11); second loan 2019-20
